open_obligations: Check that Burns et al.'s naive finetuning runs indeed use no adversarial training, which is what the citation relies on
Note that the citation is shared with [73] and [38] (weak-supervision papers), so confirm Burns et al. is cited for the weak-to-strong part of the claim
Theorem 4.3 gives guarantees only by assuming the data distribution follows a slightly more regular structure (robust expansion); check whether that assumption holds for Burns et al.'s NLP tasks

Check whether Burns et al.'s GPT-4-family students are average-case robust, as Theorem 4.3 requires, since the cited passages do not show it, and note that Burns et al. report PGR while the cited passage does not show that Theorem 4.3's guarantees are stated in terms of PGR
out.other_title: Naive weak-to-strong finetuning gives positive PGR on NLP tasks, often above 50% for the largest students
out.rationale: The authors state that their theoretical relaxation (average-case rather than adversarial robustness) is important because it matches the empirical results of Burns et al. and others that adversarial training and adversarial robustness are not required for weak-to-strong generalization to occur. The source uses the target's empirical result to motivate its theorem and gives no evidence for that result, so DEPENDS_ON rather than SUPPORTS.
out.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: Whether weak-to-strong generalization needs adversarially robust students; the source uses the empirical finding for students trained without adversarial training, with theory on one side and experiments on the other; Theorem 4.3 gives guarantees only for average-case-robust classifiers under robust expansion, whereas Burns et al. report PGR for naively finetuned students from the GPT-4 family

text: The authors extend their weak-to-strong error bounds (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2) to student classifiers that are only robust on average, under a robust-expansion assumption (Theorem 4.3). They say this generalization matters because it matches empirical results, in their references [73, 38, 10], that adversarial training and adversarial robustness are not required for weak-to-strong generalization to occur.
title: Average-case-robust weak-to-strong bounds match findings that adversarial training is not required
